title: Waves and Oscillations
subject: Physics

cards.prompt: What is Displacement? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Displacement is the change in position vector, delta r = r_final - r_initial. It depends only on the endpoints and differs from the scalar distance traveled along a path.
required_concepts: Displacement is a vector and need not equal path length.
major_error_concepts: Identifying displacement magnitude with total distance for every trajectory.

cards.prompt: What is Velocity? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Instantaneous velocity is the time derivative of position, v = dr/dt. It points tangent to the trajectory, and its magnitude is speed.
required_concepts: Speed is the magnitude of velocity.
accepted_variants: Instantaneous vector rate of change of location.
major_error_concepts: Treating speed and velocity as identical vector quantities.

cards.prompt: What is Acceleration? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Acceleration is the time derivative of velocity, a = dv/dt. It can arise from a change in speed, direction, or both; constant speed does not imply zero acceleration.
accepted_variants: Instantaneous vector rate of velocity change.
major_error_concepts: Claiming uniform circular motion has zero acceleration because speed is constant.

cards.prompt: What is Inertial Mass? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Inertial mass measures a body's resistance to acceleration under a given net force. In Newtonian mechanics with constant mass, a = F_net/m; mass is a scalar property distinct from weight.
required_concepts: Mass sets response to net force.
Mass differs from gravitational force or weight.
accepted_variants: The proportionality between net force and acceleration.
major_error_concepts: Measuring mass in newtons or treating it as location-dependent weight.

cards.prompt: What is Hooke's Law? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: In the Hooke-law regime, a spring exerts F = -k x along its deformation coordinate, where x is measured from equilibrium. The negative sign indicates a restoring direction; the linear law is valid only over a limited deformation range.
required_concepts: Force proportional to displacement from equilibrium.
Restoring sign and limited linear regime.
major_error_concepts: Using total spring length rather than extension from equilibrium as x.

cards.prompt: What is Kinetic Energy? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The translational kinetic energy of a Newtonian particle is K = one-half m v squared. It is nonnegative and depends on the reference frame through speed.
required_concepts: K = m v squared divided by two.
accepted_variants: Energy associated with particle motion in a specified frame.
major_error_concepts: Assigning negative kinetic energy merely because velocity is negative.

cards.prompt: What is Potential Energy? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A conservative force admits a potential energy U such that its work equals -delta U. Equivalently F = -gradient U where the potential is differentiable; the additive zero of U is arbitrary.
required_concepts: Conservative work equals negative potential-energy change.
Only potential differences matter to the force.
accepted_variants: Energy function whose negative gradient generates the conservative force.
major_error_concepts: Using F = positive gradient U.
Assuming potential energy must always be nonnegative.

cards.prompt: What is Mechanical Energy? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Mechanical energy is the sum of kinetic and potential energies, E_mech = K + U, for the modeled system. It need not remain constant when nonconservative interactions transfer energy into other forms.
required_concepts: Distinguish mechanical-energy conservation from total-energy conservation.
major_error_concepts: Claiming mechanical energy is conserved in every frictional process.

cards.prompt: What is Restoring Force? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A restoring force points toward a stable equilibrium when the system is displaced nearby. A linear restoring force F = -k x with k positive produces simple harmonic motion for a constant-mass undamped particle.
required_concepts: Linear restoring force is a special case.
accepted_variants: Force tending to return the coordinate toward equilibrium.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every restoring force must be exactly linear at all displacements.

cards.prompt: What is Amplitude? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Amplitude is the maximum magnitude of displacement from equilibrium in a specified oscillation. For x = A cos(omega t + phi), amplitude is the nonnegative quantity |A|.
accepted_variants: Half the peak-to-peak excursion of a symmetric sinusoidal oscillation.
major_error_concepts: Calling the distance from negative peak to positive peak the amplitude.

cards.prompt: What is Period? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Period T is the time for one complete cycle of periodic motion. For a sinusoid of angular frequency omega, T = 2 pi/omega.
major_error_concepts: Identifying period with cycles per second.

cards.prompt: What is Frequency? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Frequency f is the number of complete cycles per unit time, measured in hertz. It is the reciprocal of period: f = 1/T, while angular frequency is omega = 2 pi f.
major_error_concepts: Equating f and omega without the factor 2 pi.

cards.prompt: What is Phase? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Phase specifies a position within an oscillation's cycle. In x = A cos(omega t + phi), the total phase is omega t + phi and phi sets the initial phase relative to the chosen time origin.
required_concepts: Cycle position expressed as an angle.
Initial phase depends on time-origin and coordinate conventions.
accepted_variants: The angular argument of the sinusoidal motion.
major_error_concepts: Confusing initial phase with amplitude.

cards.prompt: What is Damping? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Damping removes energy from an oscillatory degree of freedom, commonly through a resistive term proportional to velocity. Underdamped motion oscillates with decaying amplitude; sufficiently strong damping can eliminate oscillation.
required_concepts: Damped motion need not remain oscillatory.
accepted_variants: Decay of free oscillations through energy loss.
major_error_concepts: Claiming all damped motion must oscillate forever at constant amplitude.

cards.prompt: What is Driving Force? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Driving is external forcing applied to an oscillator, often periodically. It supplies or removes energy depending on its phase relative to velocity and can maintain oscillations against damping.
required_concepts: Energy transfer depends on force and velocity phase.
accepted_variants: A driven oscillator receives an imposed time-dependent force.
major_error_concepts: Assuming a periodic drive always increases amplitude without limit.

cards.prompt: What is Local Spring Approximation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Near a stable equilibrium x0, a smooth force with nonzero restoring slope can be approximated by F(x) approximately -k_eff(x-x0), where k_eff = -F'(x0) is positive. Higher-order terms matter at larger displacements.
required_concepts: A negative force slope gives positive restoring stiffness.
accepted_variants: The leading nonzero restoring term is locally Hooke-like when the slope is nonzero.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every stable equilibrium has a nonzero quadratic potential term.

cards.prompt: What is Mechanical-Energy Conservation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Mechanical energy K + U is conserved when all working interactions in the model are conservative and no unaccounted energy transfer crosses the system boundary. Kinetic and potential energy can change individually while their sum remains fixed.
required_concepts: Conservative interactions and appropriate system boundary.
Conserved sum does not require K and U individually constant.
accepted_variants: Delta K + delta U = 0 for the conservative system.
major_error_concepts: Imposing mechanical-energy conservation across a dissipative collision without accounting for internal energy.

cards.prompt: What is Mass–Spring Period? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An ideal mass-spring oscillator with mass m and spring constant k has angular frequency sqrt(k/m) and period T = 2 pi sqrt(m/k). These are amplitude-independent within the linear, undamped model.
major_error_concepts: Claiming the ideal linear spring period increases with amplitude.

cards.prompt: What is Small-Angle Pendulum Period? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A simple pendulum of length L in uniform gravity has small-angle period T approximately 2 pi sqrt(L/g). The approximation uses sin theta approximately theta with theta in radians; finite amplitudes change the period.
major_error_concepts: Claiming the same period is exact at arbitrarily large swing amplitudes.

cards.prompt: What is Energy in Simple Harmonic Motion? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: In ideal simple harmonic motion, kinetic and quadratic potential energies exchange while their sum remains constant. Speed and kinetic energy are greatest at equilibrium; potential energy is greatest at the turning points.
required_concepts: Conserved total energy with alternating kinetic and potential contributions.
Identify equilibrium and turning-point energy roles.
accepted_variants: Periodic exchange between kinetic and restoring-potential energy.
major_error_concepts: Placing maximum speed at maximum displacement.

cards.prompt: What is Small-Angle Error Scaling? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For angles in radians, sin theta = theta - theta cubed/6 plus higher powers. Replacing sin theta by theta has absolute error of order theta cubed and relative error of order theta squared near zero.
required_concepts: Distinguish absolute cubic from relative quadratic error scaling.
accepted_variants: The leading fractional small-angle error scales with angle squared.
major_error_concepts: Applying the same coefficients to degree-valued angles.

cards.prompt: What is Potential Curvature and Stability? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: In one-dimensional conservative motion, an equilibrium satisfies U'(x0) = 0. Positive second derivative gives a local potential minimum and local stability; negative second derivative gives instability. Zero curvature requires higher-order analysis.
required_concepts: Positive curvature stable, negative unstable, zero inconclusive.
accepted_variants: Potential minima are locally stable in the conservative one-dimensional setting.
major_error_concepts: Calling every zero-curvature equilibrium stable or unstable without further information.

cards.prompt: What is Harmonic Oscillator Equation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An ideal harmonic oscillator satisfies x double prime+omega_0 squared x=0 for positive omega_0. Its acceleration is proportional and opposite to displacement, giving sinusoidal solutions about a stable equilibrium.
required_concepts: Linear acceleration-displacement relation with restoring sign.
major_error_concepts: Calling constant acceleration toward a point the harmonic-oscillator law.

cards.prompt: What is Complex Oscillation Amplitude? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A complex amplitude combines a sinusoid's magnitude and initial phase, with the real displacement obtained from a declared real-part convention such as Re[A exp(-i omega t)]. Changing the sign convention requires corresponding phase changes.
required_concepts: Complex number encodes magnitude and phase.
major_error_concepts: Combining opposite time-sign conventions without adjusting phases.

cards.prompt: What is Oscillator Phase Portrait? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An oscillator phase portrait plots displacement and velocity as state coordinates. An ideal harmonic oscillator follows closed elliptical curves whose size depends on energy, rather than tracing its sinusoidal time graph in that plane.
required_concepts: Conservative harmonic orbits are closed ellipses.
major_error_concepts: Confusing a position-versus-time sinusoid with a phase-space orbit.

cards.prompt: What is Linear Damping Equation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A linearly damped oscillator can be written x double prime+2 beta x prime+omega_0 squared x=0 with beta positive. The damping force opposes velocity, and the roots depend on beta relative to omega_0.
major_error_concepts: Treating the damping term as a position-only restoring force.

cards.prompt: What is Underdamping? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Underdamping occurs when 0<beta<omega_0 in the stated linear oscillator convention. Motion oscillates at omega_d=square root of (omega_0 squared-beta squared) with an amplitude envelope proportional to exp(-beta t).
required_concepts: Oscillatory decay with reduced frequency and exponential envelope.
accepted_variants: Weak enough damping to retain oscillation.
major_error_concepts: Using the undamped natural frequency as the exact damped frequency for nonzero beta.

cards.prompt: What is Critical Damping? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Critical damping is the repeated-root boundary beta=omega_0 between oscillatory and nonoscillatory free responses. The solution has the form (C_1+C_2 t)exp(-omega_0 t), with behavior also set by initial conditions.
major_error_concepts: Claiming every initial condition returns monotonically without crossing solely because damping is critical.

cards.prompt: What is Overdamping? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Overdamping occurs when beta>omega_0, producing two real negative characteristic roots in the standard positive-stiffness model. The motion is a sum of decaying exponentials rather than a sustained oscillation.
required_concepts: Two distinct real decay rates without sinusoidal free oscillation.
major_error_concepts: Calling an overdamped solution an oscillation at an imaginary physical frequency.

cards.prompt: What is Amplitude and Energy Decay? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: In an underdamped linear oscillator, the amplitude envelope decays as exp(-beta t). Energy scales quadratically with amplitude, so its slowly varying envelope decays as exp(-2 beta t), with cycle averaging appropriate for weak damping.
required_concepts: Amplitude and energy envelopes have different decay rates.
major_error_concepts: Using the same decay exponent for both amplitude and energy without squaring the amplitude.

cards.prompt: What is Quality Factor? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For x double prime+2 beta x prime+omega_0 squared x=0, the conventional oscillator quality factor is Q=omega_0/(2 beta). At weak damping it also measures stored energy relative to energy lost per cycle with a factor of two pi.
major_error_concepts: Interpreting high Q as faster energy decay.

cards.prompt: What is Driven Oscillator Response? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A sinusoidally driven damped oscillator has a steady displacement amplitude A=(F_0/m)/sqrt((omega_0 squared-omega squared)^2+(2 beta omega)^2). This assumes the linear model and stable damping; it describes the steady part, not every transient.
required_concepts: Response amplitude depends on detuning and damping.
major_error_concepts: Using the static displacement F_0/k as the response amplitude at all frequencies.

cards.prompt: What is Drive-Response Phase Lag? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: In the usual real-cosine convention, a damped oscillator's steady displacement lags the applied force by a phase that changes with drive frequency. At omega=omega_0 the displacement lag is pi/2 for positive damping, even though the amplitude peak may be elsewhere.
required_concepts: Quadrature at the undamped natural frequency under the stated model.
major_error_concepts: Assuming force and displacement are always in phase whenever the drive sustains motion.

cards.prompt: What is Resonance Curve? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A resonance curve plots response amplitude or another specified response measure against forcing frequency. Different measures, such as displacement and absorbed power, can peak at different frequencies, especially with appreciable damping.
required_concepts: Frequency response with specified measured quantity.
major_error_concepts: Treating all response-peak definitions as identical without specifying the observable.

cards.prompt: What is Average Driven Power? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For force F_0 cos omega t and steady displacement A cos(omega t-delta), average input power is one-half F_0 A omega sin delta. In steady state it balances average dissipated power for the modeled oscillator.
required_concepts: Average input balances dissipation in steady state.
major_error_concepts: Computing average mechanical power from force times displacement without a time derivative.

cards.prompt: What is Transient and Steady Motion? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The full linear driven response is a homogeneous transient plus a particular forced response. Stable damping causes the transient to decay, leaving the steady response; initial conditions determine the transient contribution.
major_error_concepts: Assuming switching on a drive instantly places the system in steady state.

cards.prompt: What is Resonance Bandwidth? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A resonance bandwidth is the frequency width between specified response-level points, commonly the half-power points. For a lightly damped simple oscillator, the angular-frequency half-power width is approximately 2 beta and Q approximately omega_0 divided by that width.
required_concepts: Width uses an explicit response threshold.
major_error_concepts: Using half amplitude as though it were half power for a squared-amplitude response.

cards.prompt: What is Coupled Oscillators? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Coupled oscillators exchange influence through forces connecting their coordinates. Their collective motion cannot generally be found by assigning each oscillator its isolated natural frequency unchanged.
major_error_concepts: Ignoring coupling while claiming the resulting isolated frequencies are exact collective modes.

cards.prompt: What is Normal Mode? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A normal mode is a collective linear motion with one frequency and fixed relative amplitudes among coordinates. General small motion can be superposed from modes when a suitable complete modal basis exists.
required_concepts: Common frequency with fixed relative coordinate pattern.
major_error_concepts: Calling arbitrary energy exchange between coordinates a single fixed-pattern normal mode.

cards.prompt: What is Symmetric and Antisymmetric Modes? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For two equivalent coupled oscillators with exchange symmetry, modes can often be chosen symmetric and antisymmetric under swapping the oscillators. Their frequencies depend on whether the coupling is stretched or unchanged in each motion pattern.
accepted_variants: In-phase and out-of-phase modes in the symmetric two-oscillator model.
major_error_concepts: Assuming the two mode frequencies are equal merely because the uncoupled oscillators are identical.

cards.prompt: What is Beats? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Two nearby-frequency sinusoids superpose into a fast oscillation with a slowly varying envelope. For the usual amplitude maxima, the beat frequency is the absolute difference of the two cycle frequencies.
required_concepts: Beat rate equals absolute frequency difference.
major_error_concepts: Calling the beat frequency the sum of the two input frequencies.

cards.prompt: What is Fourier Superposition? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Fourier superposition represents suitable waveforms as sums or integrals of sinusoidal components. A linear system's response can be assembled component by component when the representation and convergence assumptions apply.
major_error_concepts: Applying componentwise linear superposition to arbitrary strongly nonlinear systems unchanged.

cards.prompt: What is Harmonic Frequency? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A harmonic has a frequency equal to an integer multiple of a stated fundamental frequency. A physical system's normal modes are harmonics only when its spectrum has the required integer spacing.
major_error_concepts: Calling every normal-mode frequency an exact harmonic regardless of dispersion or boundary conditions.

cards.term: Fourier Representation of a Square Wave
cards.prompt: What is Fourier Representation of a Square Wave? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A symmetric zero-mean square wave with equal positive and negative half-cycles has a Fourier representation using odd harmonics with coefficients decaying inversely with harmonic number. The series approaches the midpoint at jumps under the standard convergence conditions.
required_concepts: Odd harmonics for the stated square-wave symmetry.
major_error_concepts: Assuming any pulse train with arbitrary duty cycle has only odd harmonics.

cards.prompt: What is Pulse Spectrum? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A localized pulse contains a range of frequency components rather than a single exact frequency. Shorter characteristic duration generally requires broader spectral support, with the precise time-bandwidth relation depending on how widths are defined.
accepted_variants: Frequency content of a transient pulse.
major_error_concepts: Calling a perfectly monochromatic infinite sinusoid a pulse localized to one finite instant.

cards.prompt: What is Wave Field? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A wave field assigns an oscillating or otherwise varying quantity to position and time. The field can represent displacement, pressure, or another physical variable, and its units and propagation equation depend on that choice.
required_concepts: Spatially and temporally varying physical field.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every wave variable is a displacement measured in meters.

cards.prompt: What is Transverse Wave? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: In a transverse mechanical wave, medium displacement is perpendicular to the propagation direction. The disturbance propagates while individual particles need not travel with the wave across the medium.
major_error_concepts: Assuming particles move along the propagation direction in a purely transverse wave.

cards.prompt: What is Longitudinal Wave? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: In a longitudinal mechanical wave, medium displacement is parallel to propagation. Compressions and rarefactions can travel through the medium while particle motion oscillates about local equilibrium.
major_error_concepts: Equating traveling compression with every particle moving continuously from source to receiver.

cards.prompt: What is Wavelength? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Wavelength is the spatial distance between neighboring equal-phase points in a periodic wave at a fixed time. It differs from amplitude, which measures the magnitude of the oscillating field variable.
required_concepts: Spatial repetition distance at fixed time.
major_error_concepts: Using crest height as wavelength.

cards.prompt: What is Wavenumber? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Angular wavenumber k is 2pi divided by wavelength and measures spatial phase change in radians per unit length. In multiple dimensions a wavevector specifies both this phase gradient and propagation geometry for a plane wave.
major_error_concepts: Using 1/lambda as angular wavenumber without acknowledging the missing two-pi convention.

cards.prompt: What is Sinusoidal Traveling Wave? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A one-dimensional sinusoidal traveling wave can be written y=A cos(kx-omega t+phi). For positive k and omega in this convention, constant-phase points move in the positive x direction.
required_concepts: Sinusoidal phase depends on position and time.
major_error_concepts: Reading propagation direction from the cosine sign without considering both spatial and temporal phase terms.

cards.prompt: What is Direction of Propagation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A profile f(x-c t) moves unchanged toward increasing x for c positive, while f(x+c t) moves toward decreasing x. Following a constant argument determines the direction without confusing particle displacement with profile motion.
major_error_concepts: Calling f(x-ct) left-moving for positive c.

cards.prompt: What is Wave-Speed Relation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For a periodic traveling wave, phase speed is c=lambda f=omega/k under the declared conventions. In a dispersive medium this speed can depend on frequency and need not equal a pulse envelope's speed.
required_concepts: Phase speed lambda times frequency or omega/k.
Distinguish group motion in dispersive media.
major_error_concepts: Assuming one phase-speed formula forces every frequency to propagate at the same speed.

cards.prompt: What is Particle Motion and Wave Motion? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Particle velocity is the time derivative of the medium displacement at a fixed material position in the small-motion model. Wave speed describes propagation of the disturbance, so it differs from the local particle velocity's magnitude and direction.
required_concepts: Local displacement derivative differs from disturbance propagation speed.
major_error_concepts: Equating a string element's transverse velocity with the wave's longitudinal propagation speed.

cards.prompt: What is Linear Wave Equation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The ideal one-dimensional linear wave equation is y_tt=c squared y_xx for constant positive c. It relates temporal acceleration to spatial curvature and supports superposed left- and right-traveling disturbances.
required_concepts: Second time derivative equals c squared times second spatial derivative.
major_error_concepts: Replacing the second time derivative by a first while claiming the same wave equation.

cards.prompt: What is D'Alembert Wave Solution? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: On an unrestricted uniform one-dimensional domain, the general sufficiently regular wave-equation solution is f(x-ct)+g(x+ct). Boundaries and initial data constrain these traveling components in a specified physical problem.
required_concepts: Sum of right- and left-traveling profiles.
major_error_concepts: Claiming a single right-moving profile represents every possible two-direction initial disturbance.

cards.prompt: What is Wave Initial Conditions? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A second-order-in-time wave equation generally requires an initial field displacement and an initial field velocity. Spatial boundary conditions are additional information, not replacements for both initial functions.
required_concepts: Two initial functions for the standard wave problem.
major_error_concepts: Assuming the initial shape alone determines every possible wave evolution.

cards.prompt: What is Wave Superposition? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For a linear homogeneous wave equation, the sum of solutions is a solution. Boundary and initial conditions must be combined consistently, and nonlinear media can violate this simple superposition principle.
required_concepts: Linearity permits addition of wave solutions.
Auxiliary conditions and linear regime matter.
major_error_concepts: Assuming arbitrary nonlinear wave amplitudes always pass through one another unchanged.

cards.prompt: What is Small-Displacement String Model? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The ideal transverse string-wave model assumes a taut flexible string, small slopes, and approximately constant tension and linear density. Under these approximations transverse force imbalance is proportional to the curvature of the string.
major_error_concepts: Using the small-slope equation as exact for large stretching that substantially changes tension.

cards.prompt: What is Linear Mass Density? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Linear mass density mu is mass per unit string length in the reference configuration. It differs from volume density and supplies the inertia per length in the string-wave equation.
major_error_concepts: Substituting volume mass density directly into a formula requiring mass per length.

cards.prompt: What is String Wave Speed? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For the ideal uniform taut string, transverse wave speed is c=sqrt(T/mu), where T is tension and mu is linear mass density. This result assumes small disturbances and the standard flexible-string approximation.
required_concepts: c=square root of tension divided by linear density.
major_error_concepts: Claiming wave speed rises with string mass density at fixed tension in this model.

cards.prompt: What is String Wave Energy Density? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: In the small-slope string model, energy per unit length is one-half mu y_t squared plus one-half T y_x squared. The first term is kinetic and the second is elastic energy associated with the displaced string shape.
required_concepts: Kinetic time-slope term plus potential spatial-slope term.
major_error_concepts: Using y squared alone as the local string strain-energy density without spatial derivatives.

cards.prompt: What is String Wave Power? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For a sinusoidal traveling wave on an ideal string, average transmitted power is one-half mu c omega squared A squared. It is power along the string, not power per area, and scales quadratically with amplitude in the linear regime.
required_concepts: Average power proportional to mu c omega squared A squared.
accepted_variants: Mean energy flux along a string.
major_error_concepts: Assuming doubling amplitude doubles rather than quadruples power at fixed frequency.

cards.prompt: What is Wave Intensity? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Wave intensity is average energy transfer per unit time per unit area normal to propagation. It is measured in power per area and should be distinguished from field amplitude and total source power.
major_error_concepts: Equating intensity numerically with amplitude regardless of medium or frequency.

cards.prompt: What is Spherical Spreading? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For an isotropic source in a lossless three-dimensional medium, fixed power spreads over spherical area 4pi r squared, giving intensity proportional to 1/r squared. This geometric decrease differs from absorption and can fail in the near field or guided geometry.
required_concepts: Power conservation over spherical area gives inverse-square intensity.
major_error_concepts: Calling all inverse-square spreading dissipative absorption.

cards.prompt: What is Wave Reflection? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Reflection sends part of an incident disturbance back from an interface or boundary. The reflected amplitude and phase depend on the field variable, impedances, and boundary conditions rather than one universal sign rule.
required_concepts: Phase and amplitude depend on conditions.
major_error_concepts: Claiming every reflected wave always reverses the same physical variable's sign.

cards.prompt: What is Fixed-End Reflection? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: At an ideal fixed string end, incident and reflected transverse displacements cancel at the boundary. The reflected displacement pulse is inverted relative to the incident pulse under the usual convention.
required_concepts: Zero boundary displacement requires inverted reflected displacement.
major_error_concepts: Claiming a fixed end permits a nonzero total displacement equal to the incident pulse alone.

cards.prompt: What is Free-End Reflection? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: At an ideal free string end with zero transverse force, the boundary slope vanishes. The reflected transverse displacement is not inverted under the standard ideal-string convention.
major_error_concepts: Applying the fixed-end displacement inversion rule unchanged to a free end.

cards.prompt: What is Wave Transmission? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Transmission carries a disturbance through an interface into a second medium. At a stationary linear interface, frequency is shared across incident and transmitted waves, while wavelength changes if phase speed changes.
required_concepts: Frequency conserved at a stationary linear interface.
major_error_concepts: Assuming wavelength must stay constant when speed changes at fixed frequency.

cards.prompt: What is String Wave Impedance? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For an ideal taut string, characteristic transverse wave impedance has magnitude Z=T/c=mu c. It relates transverse force to particle velocity for a one-way traveling wave with a declared direction and sign convention.
accepted_variants: Mechanical wave impedance of a string.
major_error_concepts: Equating wave impedance with the string's static spring constant.

cards.prompt: What is Boundary Matching? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Boundary matching enforces physical continuity or prescribed constraints at an interface, such as displacement continuity and transverse force balance for joined strings. These conditions determine reflection and transmission coefficients together.
required_concepts: Match the physical field and force or flux conditions.
major_error_concepts: Matching only displacement while ignoring force balance at a massless junction.

cards.prompt: What is Reflection and Transmission Energy Balance? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: At a passive lossless stationary interface, incident average power equals reflected plus transmitted average power. Amplitude coefficients must be converted using the appropriate impedances before interpreting them as energy fractions.
required_concepts: Power balance and impedance-dependent amplitude-to-power conversion.
major_error_concepts: Adding raw displacement amplitudes as though they were reflected and transmitted energy fractions.

cards.prompt: What is Standing Wave? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An ideal standing wave results from equal-amplitude opposite-traveling waves of the same frequency, creating fixed spatial nodes. Its pattern does not translate, and its cycle-averaged net energy flux is zero in the ideal balanced case.
required_concepts: Counterpropagating coherent waves yield stationary node pattern.
major_error_concepts: Assuming zero average net flux means there is no stored energy or local motion.

cards.prompt: What is Node? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A node is a position where the oscillation amplitude of a specified standing-wave variable is zero. A displacement node need not be a pressure node, so the field variable must be identified.
required_concepts: Zero oscillation amplitude at fixed position for stated field.
major_error_concepts: Calling nodes of every physical variable identical without examining their relation.

cards.prompt: What is Antinode? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An antinode is a position of maximum oscillation amplitude for a specified standing-wave variable. It is not necessarily a location where that variable remains constantly at its maximum instantaneous value.
major_error_concepts: Assuming an antinode never passes through equilibrium during its cycle.

cards.prompt: What is Fixed-Fixed String Modes? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An ideal string fixed at both ends has displacement nodes separated by length L and permitted wavelengths 2L/n for positive integer n. Its frequencies are n c/(2L) when the string is nondispersive.
required_concepts: Fixed-fixed boundary mode wavelengths and frequencies.
major_error_concepts: Including n=0 as an oscillatory nonzero-frequency fixed-string mode.

cards.prompt: What is Free-Free String Modes? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An ideal free-free string has zero-slope boundary conditions and oscillatory mode frequencies n c/(2L) for positive integers n. A separate zero-frequency uniform translation mode exists in the ideal unconstrained transverse model.
required_concepts: Free-end slope conditions and positive-integer frequency series.
major_error_concepts: Calling the uniform displacement mode a finite-frequency harmonic oscillation.

cards.prompt: What is Fixed-Free String Modes? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An ideal string with one fixed and one free end has a displacement node at one end and antinode at the other. Its permitted frequencies are (2n-1)c/(4L) for positive integer n, giving odd multiples of the fundamental.
required_concepts: Node-antinode ends and odd quarter-wave sequence.
major_error_concepts: Using the fixed-fixed half-wave fundamental unchanged for fixed-free boundaries.

cards.prompt: What is Normal Modes and Harmonics? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Normal modes are the independent oscillation patterns of a linear boundary-value problem. Harmonics are integer frequency multiples; these categories coincide for some ideal strings and pipes but not for every dispersive or geometrically different resonator.
required_concepts: Mode structure differs from integer frequency classification.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every resonator has exactly integer-spaced normal-mode frequencies.

cards.prompt: What is Continuous Frequency Spectrum? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An unbounded ideal propagation domain can support a continuum of wavenumbers rather than the discrete spectrum imposed by confining boundaries. A localized disturbance is then represented using an integral over modes or frequencies.
required_concepts: Unconfined domains can admit continuous modal parameters.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every wave field has only integer multiples of one fundamental frequency.

cards.prompt: What is Resonator? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A resonator stores wave energy in modes selected by its geometry and boundaries. Losses limit mode lifetime and broaden resonances, while coupling determines how external forcing injects or extracts energy.
required_concepts: Boundary-selected energy-storing modes with losses and coupling.
major_error_concepts: Assuming a cavity's geometry alone sets its resonance width regardless of losses.

cards.prompt: What is Acoustic Pressure? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Acoustic pressure is the small pressure deviation from an equilibrium background associated with a sound disturbance. It is not the full ambient pressure and can oscillate positively and negatively relative to that background.
required_concepts: Pressure perturbation relative to ambient equilibrium.
major_error_concepts: Interpreting a negative acoustic pressure perturbation as necessarily negative absolute pressure.

cards.prompt: What is Acoustic Particle Velocity? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Acoustic particle velocity is the local fluid velocity perturbation accompanying sound. In ordinary small-amplitude longitudinal sound it is parallel to propagation for a single plane wave, but its magnitude is far smaller than sound speed in the linear regime.
required_concepts: Fluid motion perturbation distinct from propagation speed.
major_error_concepts: Identifying acoustic particle speed with the speed of sound.

cards.prompt: What is Bulk Modulus? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Bulk modulus measures resistance to uniform compression, B=-V dP/dV under the specified thermodynamic condition. Sound-speed calculations use the modulus appropriate to the compression timescale, commonly adiabatic for the ideal acoustic model.
required_concepts: Pressure response to fractional volume compression.
major_error_concepts: Using an unspecified bulk modulus while ignoring whether compression is isothermal or adiabatic.

cards.prompt: What is Sound Speed in a Fluid? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The speed of small longitudinal sound waves in a uniform fluid is c=sqrt(B/rho) with the appropriate compressional modulus and equilibrium mass density. For an ideal gas in the adiabatic model, B=gamma P.
required_concepts: Sound speed from compressional modulus divided by mass density.
major_error_concepts: Substituting string linear density into the fluid sound-speed formula.

cards.prompt: What is Plane-Wave Acoustic Impedance? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For a one-way plane sound wave in a lossless uniform fluid, pressure and longitudinal particle velocity have characteristic impedance magnitude Z=rho c. The sign relation depends on direction, and standing or reactive near fields need not obey the same simple scalar ratio locally.
required_concepts: Plane progressive-wave pressure-to-velocity ratio rho c.
accepted_variants: Specific acoustic impedance of a progressive plane wave.
major_error_concepts: Applying p/u=rho c pointwise to every standing-wave node without qualification.

cards.prompt: What is Acoustic Intensity? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Average acoustic intensity is the cycle average of pressure perturbation times particle velocity in the propagation direction. For a single sinusoidal progressive plane wave it is p_rms squared/(rho c), equivalently peak pressure squared/(2rho c).
major_error_concepts: Using peak pressure squared/(rho c) while claiming the RMS-based intensity formula.

cards.prompt: What is Decibel Intensity Level? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An intensity level in decibels is 10 log base 10 of I divided by a stated positive reference intensity. Doubling intensity raises the level by about 3 dB, and a decibel level is a logarithmic ratio rather than an absolute intensity unit by itself.
major_error_concepts: Using 20 log10 for an intensity ratio rather than an amplitude ratio under equal impedance.

cards.prompt: What is Sound Pressure Level? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Sound pressure level is 20 log base 10 of RMS pressure divided by a stated reference pressure. Converting it to intensity requires assumptions about impedance and wave type, so pressure level and intensity level are not universally interchangeable.
required_concepts: Intensity conversion depends on acoustic conditions.
major_error_concepts: Claiming pressure level alone specifies energy flux in any standing or near field.

cards.prompt: What is Open-Open Pipe Modes? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An ideal open-open air column has pressure nodes near both ends and frequencies n c/(2L) for positive integers n, ignoring end corrections. Displacement and particle-velocity antinodes correspond approximately to those open-end pressure nodes.
major_error_concepts: Calling an open pipe end a pressure antinode in the ideal boundary model.

cards.prompt: What is Closed-Open Pipe Modes? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An ideal closed-open air column has a pressure antinode at the closed end and node at the open end. Its frequencies are (2n-1)c/(4L), neglecting end corrections and other nonideal effects.
required_concepts: Closed pressure antinode and open pressure node.
major_error_concepts: Using a pressure node at a rigid closed end in the ideal pipe model.

cards.prompt: What is Acoustic End Correction? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Acoustic end correction accounts for an open-end effective pressure boundary lying outside the pipe's geometric end. It changes effective resonating length and depends on opening geometry and frequency regime rather than one universal added length.
required_concepts: Effective acoustic length differs from geometric length near open end.
major_error_concepts: Applying one geometry-independent correction to every opening and frequency.

cards.prompt: What is Doppler Effect? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The Doppler effect is a change in received frequency caused by relative motion of source, observer, or propagation environment. For sound, velocities relative to the medium matter, so moving source and moving observer effects are not generally interchangeable.
major_error_concepts: Using only source-observer relative speed for every acoustic Doppler setup without considering the medium.

cards.prompt: What is Moving Sound Source? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A sound source moving through a stationary medium changes the spacing of emitted wavefronts. Ahead of a subsonic source of speed v_s, wavelength is (c-v_s)/f_source in the simple collinear constant-speed model.
required_concepts: Source motion changes emitted spatial spacing.
major_error_concepts: Using the forward wavelength formula unchanged behind the source.

cards.prompt: What is Moving Sound Observer? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An observer moving toward incoming wavefronts encounters them more frequently. For a stationary source and a collinear observer approaching through still medium, received frequency is f_source(c+v_o)/c, with v_o defined positive toward the source.
major_error_concepts: Treating observer motion as changing the source's emitted wavelength in the stationary medium.

cards.prompt: What is Shock and Mach Cone? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A source moving faster than sound in a uniform medium can generate a Mach cone, with sin mu=c/v_source=1/M for the ideal steady geometry. The cone is the envelope of disturbances, not a prediction of infinite physical amplitude from the ordinary subsonic Doppler formula.
required_concepts: Supersonic cone geometry with sin angle=1/M.
major_error_concepts: Extending a divergent subsonic Doppler expression as a complete description of a supersonic shock.

cards.prompt: What is Dispersion Relation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A dispersion relation connects angular frequency and wavenumber for a medium and wave type, commonly omega=omega(k). It determines phase and envelope propagation and can have several branches in coupled or multi-mode systems.
major_error_concepts: Assuming the relation must always be omega=c k with one constant c.

cards.prompt: What is Phase Velocity? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Phase velocity is omega/k for a one-dimensional monochromatic wave and tracks a constant-phase point. It need not equal the speed of energy transfer or a localized signal envelope in a dispersive medium.
major_error_concepts: Calling phase speed automatically the speed of every pulse or information front.

cards.prompt: What is Group Velocity? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Group velocity is d omega/dk in one dimension for a narrowband packet on a smooth dispersion branch. It describes envelope motion under the appropriate approximation, while strongly distorted or lossy packets can require more careful interpretation.
required_concepts: Derivative of dispersion relation for narrowband envelope motion.
major_error_concepts: Replacing d omega/dk with omega/k in every dispersive medium.

cards.prompt: What is Wave Packet? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A wave packet superposes a band of nearby wavenumbers to create a localized envelope. The carrier phase and envelope can move differently when the dispersion relation is nonlinear.
required_concepts: Localized superposition with finite wavenumber spread.
major_error_concepts: Assuming a finite localized packet consists of one exact wavenumber only.

cards.prompt: What is Dispersive Packet Spreading? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Dispersive packet spreading occurs when nearby spectral components have different propagation behavior, causing an initially localized envelope to change width or shape. The curvature of the dispersion relation is important for narrowband spreading.
major_error_concepts: Attributing all packet broadening to absorption rather than possible dispersion.

cards.prompt: What is Nondispersive Propagation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A nondispersive branch has frequency proportional to wavenumber over the relevant band, giving equal constant phase and group speeds there. Its ideal traveling profiles can propagate without dispersive distortion, though losses or boundaries can still change them.
required_concepts: Linear frequency-wavenumber relation and equal speeds in the band.
major_error_concepts: Assuming nondispersive automatically means lossless or reflection-free.

cards.prompt: What is Surface-Wave Dispersion? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Surface-water waves can be dispersive because gravity, surface tension, and depth contribute differently across wavelengths. The familiar long shallow-water gravity-wave limit is approximately nondispersive, unlike many shorter-wavelength regimes.
required_concepts: Wave regime depends on gravity, surface tension, depth, and wavelength.
major_error_concepts: Assigning one wavelength-independent speed to every water wave in every depth.

cards.prompt: What is Polarization? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Polarization describes the direction and time evolution of a transverse wave's vector oscillation at a point. Linear, circular, and elliptical polarization correspond to different component amplitudes and relative phases; a scalar longitudinal sound wave does not have the same transverse polarization freedom.
major_error_concepts: Defining ordinary longitudinal fluid sound polarization by rotating an independent transverse displacement vector.

cards.prompt: What is Coherence? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Coherence characterizes a stable statistical phase relationship across time or positions sufficient for reproducible interference. Equal nominal frequencies alone do not guarantee coherence if relative phase drifts randomly over the measurement interval.
required_concepts: Stable or correlated relative phase across relevant interval.
major_error_concepts: Assuming two unrelated same-frequency sources necessarily yield stationary interference fringes.

cards.prompt: What is Interference? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Interference is the change in the resultant field from superposing waves with different relative phases. In a linear field, amplitudes add first and intensity follows the appropriate quadratic relation, including cross terms when coherence is present.
required_concepts: Relative phase and coherence control cross terms.
major_error_concepts: Adding intensities directly for coherent waves while ignoring interference cross terms.

cards.prompt: What is Path Difference and Phase Difference? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For waves of the same wavelength in a common medium, a path difference delta l contributes phase difference 2pi delta l/lambda. Source phase and any reflection-induced phase changes must also be included.
required_concepts: Propagation phase difference from path difference.
major_error_concepts: Using path difference alone when one path includes an additional phase-inverting reflection.

cards.prompt: What is Destructive Interference and Energy? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Destructive interference reduces the resultant field in a region when waves oppose in phase. It does not by itself destroy energy; full energy accounting includes redistribution, standing-wave storage, and the source-boundary arrangement.
required_concepts: Local cancellation differs from energy destruction.
accepted_variants: Interference cancellation with global energy accounting.
major_error_concepts: Claiming canceled displacement proves energy has vanished from the full physical system.

cards.prompt: What is Diffraction? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Diffraction is the spreading and interference of waves around apertures or obstacles when boundary geometry shapes propagation. Its importance depends on wavelength relative to feature size; geometrical-ray approximations become limited when those scales are comparable.
accepted_variants: Wave bending and spreading beyond simple rays.
major_error_concepts: Assuming waves cannot reach any region beyond an obstacle's straight-line geometric shadow.

cards.prompt: What is Huygens Principle? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Huygens' construction treats a wavefront as a source of secondary wavelets whose combined propagation builds later wavefronts. Quantitative diffraction requires the appropriate amplitudes, phases, and boundary conditions, not merely drawing expanding circles.
major_error_concepts: Treating a geometric wavelet sketch alone as a complete quantitative diffraction calculation.

cards.prompt: What is Attenuation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Attenuation reduces wave amplitude through losses or other specified mechanisms along propagation. If amplitude decays as exp(-alpha x) in a fixed-impedance model, intensity decays as exp(-2 alpha x); this differs from geometric spreading alone.
required_concepts: Amplitude loss and squared-amplitude intensity relation.
major_error_concepts: Using the same exponent for amplitude and intensity while defining alpha as the amplitude attenuation coefficient.

cards.prompt: What is Nonlinear Wave Propagation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Nonlinear wave propagation occurs when the field amplitude changes the governing response so superposition no longer holds exactly. It can generate harmonics, steepening, or other interactions, depending on the medium and regime.
major_error_concepts: Assuming the linear superposition principle remains exact at arbitrary amplitude.

cards.prompt: What is Wave Measurement Resolution? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Wave measurements have finite observation duration, spatial aperture, sampling interval, and sensor response. These limit frequency resolution and measurable bandwidth, so an apparent spectral peak or missing mode must be interpreted with the measurement window and excitation in mind.
required_concepts: Finite sampling and observation windows constrain wave inference.
accepted_variants: Resolution and bandwidth of a wave measurement.
major_error_concepts: Interpreting absence of a measured peak as proof no mode exists without considering excitation and detector response.

description: A definition-recall course deck covering core concepts in Waves and Oscillations.
